chapter.title: Values
chapter.para: Rexx has one kind of value, the string, and whether it is a number depends on how it is used; .NET has types, and its methods say which they take. So a Rexx string becomes whatever the parameter it goes to wants, and .NET's simple values come back as Rexx strings. Everything else crosses by reference: a .NET object is a NetObject in Rexx, and a Rexx object a RexxObject in .NET.

section.title: From Rexx to .NET
section.para: The member is chosen first (), and then each argument is converted to its parameter's type:

row.entry: the parameter's type: a string as it is ("007" stays "007"); an integer type the number fits exactly, with no rounding and no truncation ("007" is 7 for an int, 3.7 fits no integer type); a double, float or decimal any number in its range, rounded to its precision, but not one too large for it nor one that is not zero and would be read as zero (1E-999: the error says 1E-999 is out of range for a Double), and, for a double or float, nan, +infinity and -infinity by name; a bool from 1 or 0 (or true, false); a char from one character; an enum from a name or a number; DateTime, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpan and Guid by their culture-invariant parsing; for an object parameter (or a generic type parameter not otherwise known), a string
a LogicalWrapper (.LogicalWrapper~true, ~false; the booleans of json.cls and yaml.cls)
a bool, also to an object parameter (or an interface bool implements); to any other parameter, as its string, 1 or 0 ()
null, for a reference type or a nullable value type
its .NET object; a NetType gives its System.Type where one is wanted
a delegate of the parameter's type ()
a ref, out or in argument ()

for an array, a List<T> or an IEnumerable<T> parameter, a new one with the items converted (a copy); a multidimensional Array, a .NET array of the same rank; for a RexxObject parameter, the Array itself ()

for a dictionary with string keys (Dictionary<string, T>, IDictionary<string, T>, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, T>, IDictionary), a new Dictionary<string, T>, the values converted (a copy); for any other parameter, by reference, as the next row
a RexxObject, by reference, which .NET code can keep and send messages to (); it comes back to Rexx as itself

section.para: A string that the parameter cannot take makes that overload fail; if no overload is left, the call is an error naming the candidates.

example.title: Rexx strings given to .NET
example.programlisting:
sb = .net~System~Text~StringBuilder~new sb~Append("007")~Append(" ")~Append(.net~int32("007")) say sb~ToString -- Append(string), then Append(int) say .net~System~TimeSpan~FromMinutes(90)~ToString say .net~System~DateTime~new(2026, 10, 16)~AddDays(1)~ToString("yyyy-MM-dd") say .net~System~Char~IsDigit("7") .net~System~String~IsNullOrEmpty(.nil)
::requires "net.cls"

example.title: Numbers out of range for a double
example.programlisting:
m = .net~System~Math say m~Sqrt("5E-324") m~Sqrt("+infinity") -- a subnormal, an infinity by name signal on syntax say m~Sqrt("1E-999") -- not zero, but a double would make it 0 syntax: say condition("O")~message~left(36)
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: 2.2227587494850775E-162 +infinity 1E-999 is out of range for a Double:

section.para: A Rexx string prefers a string parameter when the overloads offer one: .net~System~Convert~ToBoolean(1) calls ToBoolean(string), which wants "True" or "False", and fails. Force the type the call means: .net~System~Convert~ToBoolean(.net~int32(1)). Indexers are the one exception ().

section.title: Forcing a Type
section.para: When the choice must be the program's, an argument can carry a .NET type: .net~int16(x), int32, int64, uint16, uint32, uint64, byte, sbyte, single, double, decimal, char and string, .net~null (a null of no particular type), and any type with .net~as(x, type), the type a name or a NetType (an enum, a nullable type, an interface, a delegate type for a NetHandler). Each answers a , which marks the value: the conversion happens at the call, and fails there if the value does not fit the type. .net~bool(x) answers a LogicalWrapper instead ().

example.title: Forcing a type
example.programlisting:
c = .net~System~Convert say c~ToBoolean(.net~int32(1)) c~ToBoolean("False") say c~ToString(.net~as(255, "byte"), 2) say c~ToString(.net~int16(-1), 16) c~ToString(.net~int32(-1), 16)
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: Booleans
section.para: &true; and &false; are the strings 1 and 0: nothing tells &false; from the number 0. So the bridge uses ooRexx's class LogicalWrapper (logicalwrapper.cls, since r13278; net.cls requires it), which every ooRexx bridge uses for its host's booleans. It has two instances, .LogicalWrapper~true and .LogicalWrapper~false, which behave as 1 and 0 wherever Rexx uses a value (IF, operators, comparisons, string methods, SAY, indexes); isA(.LogicalWrapper) tells them apart, and .LogicalWrapper~of(a > b) gives the one for a logical value. Its subclasses, JSONBoolean (json.cls) and YamlBoolean (yaml.cls), are booleans too: what those packages read reaches .NET as bools. A program that names the class needs ::requires "logicalwrapper.cls" (or net.cls, which requires it).

listitem.para: A .NET bool comes to Rexx as one of them, so it goes back to .NET as a bool, also to an object parameter or into a List<object>.

Any object that isA(.LogicalWrapper) goes as a bool; where overloads compete, the one that takes a bool wins (Convert.ToString(.LogicalWrapper~false) is False). To a parameter of another type it goes as its string.
.net~bool(x) gives the instance for 1, 0, true or false (caseless).
A COM method gets a LogicalWrapper as VT_BOOL, as &true; and &false; themselves.

example.title: Booleans
example.programlisting:
empty = .net~System~String~IsNullOrEmpty("") say empty empty~class~id (empty = .true) (\empty) c = .net~System~Convert say c~ToString(.LogicalWrapper~false) c~ToString(.false) c~ToString(.net~bool("true")) list = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<object>")~new list~Add(empty); list~Add(1) say list[0]~isA(.LogicalWrapper) list[1]~isA(.LogicalWrapper) say c~ToString(.json~new~fromJSON("[false]")[1])
::requires "net.cls" ::requires "json.cls"

section.title: Boxed Values
section.para: .net~box(type, x) goes further than a forced type: it makes a .NET object that holds x as that type, and gives it as a NetObject, by reference. A box is the .NET value: it goes to .NET as itself (an object parameter sees an Int16), and it can be kept, put in a collection and passed around. .net~unbox(o) gives its Rexx value back. The type is a NetType or any name type takes, or one of BSF4ooRexx's indicators, as every ooRexx bridge takes them: BOolean, BYte, Char, Double, Float, Int, Long, Object, SHort, STring, caseless and shortened down to their capitals ("I", "d"), or one of CLR.CLS's ("INT16", "DE" for Decimal, "SI" for Single). BYte is .NET's Byte, unsigned (Java's signed byte is SByte). See .

example.title: Boxed values
example.programlisting:
b = .net~box("short", 5) say .net~typeOf(b) .net~unbox(b) say .net~typeOf(.net~box("I", 5)) .net~typeOf(.net~box("DE", 5)) l = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<object>")~new l~Add(5); l~Add(.net~box("int", 5)); l~Add(.net~int16(5)) e = .net~System~Linq~Enumerable -- what the List holds: say .net~invoke(e, "OfType<string>", l)~makeArray~items - .net~invoke(e, "OfType<int>", l)~makeArray~items - .net~invoke(e, "OfType<short>", l)~makeArray~items
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: From .NET to Rexx

row.entry: every numeric type, BigInteger, Int128, UInt128 and Half included

a string with the number, culture-invariant: whole numbers with all their digits (a BigInteger of any size), a double or float with its shortest digits that read back as the same value, written as Rexx writes x + 0 under NUMERIC DIGITS 17: plain digits (0.0000001, 10000000000000000) unless the integer part needs more than 17 places or the decimals more than 34 (1E+17, 1E-35), no .0 on a whole value (1), -0 kept, and NaN and the infinities as ooRexx writes them, nan, +infinity and -infinity (which go back to a double as they are; .NET's own spellings, NaN and Infinity, do too); a decimal with its digits
.LogicalWrapper~true or .LogicalWrapper~false, which are 1 and 0 to Rexx ()
a NetEnum, whose string value is its name ()
a NetArray, which behaves as a Rexx Array, from 1 ()
a Rexx object that had gone to .NET (a RexxObject)
any other object (structs, Complex among them, collections, delegates, tasks, types)
a NetObject, by reference; a type is a NetType

section.para: A boxed number, bool, char or string (an object that holds one) comes as its value, like an unboxed one: a box that goes to .NET and comes back is a Rexx string again.

example.title: .NET values in Rexx
example.programlisting:
m = .net~System~Math say m~Sqrt(2) m~PI say m~Pow(10, -7) m~Pow(10, 17) m~Pow(2, 53) m~Round(-0.4) -- as Rexx writes them say .net~System~Double~NaN .net~System~Double~PositiveInfinity say .net~System~Int64~MaxValue .net~System~UInt64~MaxValue say 1/3 .net~System~Decimal~Divide(1, 3) x = .net~System~Numerics~BigInteger~Pow(2, 100) -- a Rexx number, all its digits numeric digits 40; say x x + 1 x~datatype("W"); numeric digits say .net~System~Environment~GetEnvironmentVariable("NO_SUCH_VARIABLE") == .nil
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: By Reference
section.para: Objects are never copied. A NetObject holds a handle to its .NET object, which keeps the object alive while Rexx holds the proxy; when Rexx collects the proxy, its uninit releases the handle. The same .NET object, however it comes to Rexx, gives proxies that are == to each other, and a proxy goes back to .NET as the object itself. The same holds the other way: a Rexx object given to .NET is a RexxObject there, and comes back to Rexx as itself.
The copies are the conversions that a parameter's type asks for: a Rexx Array to a .NET array or list, a StringTable or a Directory to a dictionary. What .NET then changes in the copy stays in .NET.

example.title: Objects by reference
example.programlisting:
l = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<object>")~new d = .directory~new sb = .net~System~Text~StringBuilder~new l~Add(d); l~Add(sb) say (l[0] == d) (l[1] == sb) (l[1]~Append("x") == sb) say sb~ToString
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: Numbers, Dates and the Culture
section.para: What the bridge converts does not depend on the machine: a Rexx number goes to a double, decimal or integer parameter as Rexx writes it (with a point), and a .NET number comes back the same way, on any Windows, Linux or macOS. But the bridge does not change .NET's own culture: a .NET method that reads text as a number or a date, or writes one as text, uses the culture of the machine (CultureInfo.CurrentCulture, from Windows' regional settings) unless it is given another. On a Spanish Windows the point separates thousands, so a Rexx number given to such a method as text is read wrongly: .net~System~Convert~ToDouble("0.5") is 5 there, and nothing warns.

.NET's methods that read or write text have an overload with one argument more, an IFormatProvider: a CultureInfo is one, and CultureInfo.InvariantCulture is the culture that is the same everywhere (a point, English names). Give it whenever the text is a Rexx number or is meant for a program; give none (or the user's) when the text is for a person.

Often the simplest is not to let .NET read the text at all: a number whose type is forced (.net~double(x), ) is converted by the bridge, with no culture. The conversions the bridge makes itself are culture-invariant too where .NET has a culture: DateTime, TimeSpan and the like from a Rexx string (). The COM bridge calls in English, as VBA does ().

example.title: The culture, given
example.programlisting:
inv = .net~System~Globalization~CultureInfo~InvariantCulture es = .net~System~Globalization~CultureInfo~GetCultureInfo("es-ES") say .net~System~Convert~ToDouble("0.5", inv) .net~System~Double~Parse("1E3", inv) x = .net~box("double", 1234.5) -- a .NET double, with its methods say x~ToString("N2", inv) "/" x~ToString("N2", es) say .net~System~String~Format(inv, "{0:N1} {1:P0}", x, .net~double(0.25)) d = .net~System~DateTime~new(2026, 10, 18) say d~ToString("D", inv) "/" d~ToString("D", es) say .net~System~DateTime~ParseExact("18/10/2026", "dd/MM/yyyy", inv)~DayOfYear
::requires "net.cls"
